tip: ‘lle’ joins a place to what happened there, like where: ‘yr ysgol lle dysgodd hi’ = the school where she learned.
‘taw’ marks a reported emphasis in south Welsh, like that it was: ‘dwedodd hi taw hi’ = she said it was her.
‘beidio â’ means not to; after ‘â’ the next p, t or c adds an h, so ‘poeni’ becomes ‘phoeni’ in ‘beidio â phoeni’.
‘a’ opens an indirect yes or no question, like whether: ‘gofynnodd ... a oedd’ = asked whether it was.
‘cyn i’ means before; the verb after softens, so ‘dod’ becomes ‘ddod’: ‘cyn i'r gaeaf ddod’ = before winter comes.
‘pe na bai’ means if it weren't; ‘pe’ sets an unreal condition and ‘na’ makes it negative: ‘pe na bai'n bwrw glaw’.
‘-af’ (often ‘-a’ in speech) marks most or -est: ‘poeth’ (hot) becomes ‘poetha’, hottest, in ‘y diwrnod poetha'r flwyddyn’.
‘a’ opens a yes or no question and softens the next word: ‘byddai’ becomes ‘fyddai’ in ‘a fyddai'n bosib’ = would it be possible.
‘dy’ (your) softens the next consonant: ‘car’ becomes ‘gar’ and ‘beic’ becomes ‘feic’ in ‘dy gar a dy feic’.
‘taw’ points to the emphasised bit, a southern form of ‘mai’: ‘taw hi oedd yno’ stresses it was her, not someone else, who was there.
‘wedi’ marks a completed action and replaces the present-tense ‘yn’: ‘dw i wedi bwcio’ = I have booked.
‘unrhyw’ (any) softens the next word: ‘problem’ becomes ‘broblem’ in ‘unrhyw broblem’.
putting the pronoun ‘fe’ before ‘oedd’ marks emphasis: ‘fe oedd wedi awgrymu’ = it was him, not another, who suggested it.
‘gyda'n gilydd’ means together; ‘gilydd’ (each other) takes a group marker, here ‘'n’ for our.
‘lle’ joins a place to what happened there, as where: ‘dyna'r pentref lle tyfais i’ = that's the village where I grew up.
Welsh shows possession by putting nouns side by side, with no word for of: ‘gwariant y llywodraeth’ = the government's spending.
‘y byddai’ carries the reported would: ‘dywedodd e y byddai'n ffonio’ = he said that he would phone.
‘a’ (and) adds an h to a following p, t or c: ‘tywyll’ becomes ‘thywyll’ in ‘oer a thywyll’ = cold and dark.
the linking ‘yn’ softens a following describing word: ‘trist’ becomes ‘yn drist’, ‘da’ becomes ‘yn dda’.
a singular feminine noun softens after ‘'r’ (the): ‘gardd’ becomes ‘'r ardd’ = the garden.
‘eisoes’ (already) sits just before ‘wedi’: ‘mae hi eisoes wedi bwcio’ = she has already booked.
here ‘'n’ is short for ‘ein’ (our): ‘bwyta'n cinio’ = eat our lunch.
Welsh often drops the relative word that: ‘dyna'r mynydd dringais i’ = that's the mountain I climbed.
‘na’ means than after a comparison: ‘yn hirach na'r disgwyl’ = longer than expected.
‘fod’ means that in reported speech: ‘darllennais i fod y pris wedi codi’ = I read that the price had risen.
‘ymuno’ takes ‘â’ (with), not a plain object: ‘ymunodd ein ffrindiau â ni’ = our friends joined us.
‘newydd’ before a verb means have just, and softens it: ‘newydd orffen’ (from ‘gorffen’) = have just finished.
‘fy’ wraps the verb and changes its first sound (d to n): ‘dysgu’ becomes ‘fy nysgu i’ = taught me.
the ‘-ir’ ending says something is done with no named doer: ‘derbynnir ceisiadau’ = applications are accepted.
the ‘-af’ ending forms the -est (most) word: ‘ieuengaf’ = youngest, from the irregular ‘ifanc’ (young).
